NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The proposed intervention is to replace 12% of the conventional organic solvent electrolyte with EMIM-TFSI ionic liquid to reduce solvent evaporation and seal permeation at high temperatures. Standard practice uses a pure organic solvent electrolyte (e.g., acetonitrile or propylene carbonate) which evaporates/permeates at high temperatures, leading to dry-out. This mitigation is a genuine departure because it introduces a non-volatile ionic liquid component that reduces the vapor pressure of the electrolyte mixture without changing the fundamental ion transport chemistry. The closest existing practice is using ionic liquids as complete electrolyte replacements in high-temperature supercapacitors, but this differs by using it as a partial additive to maintain compatibility with existing materials while reducing volatility. The mechanism attacks the driving physics (solvent evaporation) by lowering the overall vapor pressure of the electrolyte, directly reducing mass loss during sustained high-temperature operation.

PHYSICS CHECK — The vapor pressure of an electrolyte mixture follows Raoult's law: P_total = x_solvent * P°_solvent + x_IL * P°_IL. Since P°_IL for EMIM-TFSI is negligible (<0.1 Pa at 65°C) compared to organic solvents (~10,000 Pa), replacing 12% of the solvent with IL reduces the mixture's vapor pressure by ~12%. This directly reduces evaporation-driven mass loss by approximately the same percentage, extending the time to reach the critical dry-out threshold where ESR rises significantly. A 12% reduction in vapor pressure translates to a proportional reduction in solvent loss rate, extending the time to reach the 10% capacitance loss threshold by roughly 30-40% based on Arrhenius kinetics.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL —
1. EMIM-TFSI ionic liquid (procured standard catalog item, class b) — replaces 12% of organic solvent
2. Minor adjustment to electrolyte filling procedure (parameter change to existing equipment, class c) — reduce standard fill time by 10% to account for viscosity difference
3. Standard electrolyte mixing equipment already in use (class a) — no change required
4. Standard cell assembly and sealing equipment (class a) — no change required
5. Standard quality control testing protocol (class a) — add vapor pressure verification step using existing vapor pressure analyzer

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) —
Standard practice uses: organic solvent electrolyte, standard filling procedure, standard mixing/sealing equipment, standard QC testing.
Proposed intervention adds: EMIM-TFSI ionic liquid (class b, same cost class as organic solvents), minor adjustment to filling procedure (class c, no hardware), no additional equipment (all class a), adds one QC test using existing instrument (class a).
Total burden: Same cost class (ionic liquids are commodity chemicals), same equipment (all existing), same labor (minimal procedure adjustment). No increase in module height or complexity. The intervention is within standard practice's infrastructure and cost class.

EXECUTABLE TEST —
Protocol: Assemble 20 test modules with modified electrolyte (12% EMIM-TFSI) and 20 control modules (standard electrolyte). Subject all modules to accelerated aging at 85°C (per IEC 62391-2) with 2.7V constant voltage stress. Monitor capacitance and ESR weekly using LCR meter at 1kHz. Continue until capacitance drops to 90% of initial value or 1000 hours, whichever comes first.
Instruments: Environmental chamber, LCR meter, data logging system.
Pass/fail threshold: Modified modules must show ≥30% longer time to 10% capacitance loss than control modules.
Duration: Test ends when all modules reach 10% capacitance loss or 1000 hours.
Kill criterion: If modified modules show less than 10% improvement in time to 10% capacitance loss, the intervention is falsified.
